Moment representations for generalized Lehmer polynomials

Karin Ikeda Karin IkedaInstitute of Mathematics for Industry, Kyushu University, Motooka 744, Nishi-ku, Fukuoka 819-0395, Japan Email address: ikeda@imi.kyushu-u.ac.jp and Hideki Murahara Hideki MuraharaThe University of Kitakyushu, 4-2-1 Kitagata, Kokuraminami-ku, Kitakyushu, Fukuoka, 802-8577, Japan Email address: hmurahara@mathformula.page
Abstract.

We represent normalized generalized Lehmer polynomials as moments of a random variable constructed from two independent negative binomial variables and an independent uniform variable. An integral form of their known exponential generating function yields mixtures of uniform distributions and convergent double series. We recover Eulerian polynomial identities and give a probabilistic interpretation of anti-diagonal sums of poly-Bernoulli numbers. We also prove moment determinacy, characterize the Stieltjes parameter range, derive Hankel total non-negativity and log-convexity, and identify the boundary distributions.

Key words and phrases: 
Central binomial series, generalized Lehmer polynomial, negative binomial distribution, moment representation, poly-Bernoulli number, Stieltjes moment sequence
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11B68; Secondary 05A19, 60E05, 44A60

1. Introduction

1.1. Central binomial series

The central binomial series

ζC​B​(s)≔∑m=1∞1(2​mm)​ms\zeta_{CB}(s)\coloneqq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\binom{2m}{m}m^{s}}

converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℂ\mathbb{C}, and hence defines an entire function. Its values at non-positive integers lie in ℚ+ℚ​π/3\mathbb{Q}+\mathbb{Q}\pi/\sqrt{3}. Lehmer [8] introduced the polynomials pn​(z)p_{n}(z) and qn​(z)q_{n}(z) defined by the initial values p−1​(z)=0p_{-1}(z)=0 and q−1​(z)=1q_{-1}(z)=1 and the recurrences, valid for n≥−1n\geq-1,

(1.1) qn+1​(z)\displaystyle q_{n+1}(z) =(2​(n+1)​z+1)​qn​(z)+2​z​(1−z)​qn′​(z),\displaystyle=(2(n+1)z+1)q_{n}(z)+2z(1-z)q_{n}^{\prime}(z),
pn+1​(z)\displaystyle p_{n+1}(z) =2​(n​z+1)​pn​(z)+2​z​(1−z)​pn′​(z)+qn​(z),\displaystyle=2(nz+1)p_{n}(z)+2z(1-z)p_{n}^{\prime}(z)+q_{n}(z),

and showed that, for every integer k≥1k\geq 1,

ζC​B​(1−k)=(23)k​{12​pk−1​(14)+π3​3​qk−1​(14)}.\zeta_{CB}(1-k)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{k}\left\{\frac{1}{2}p_{k-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}q_{k-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\right\}.

Borwein, Broadhurst, and Kamnitzer [5] showed, through log-sine integrals, that for every integer k≥2k\geq 2 the value ζC​B​(k)\zeta_{CB}(k) is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear combination of multiple zeta values, multiple Clausen values, and multiple Glaisher values. Bényi and Matsusaka [4], Theorems 2.4 and 3.8, express Lehmer’s polynomials in terms of bivariate Eulerian polynomials. Their Theorem 3.6 proves Stephan’s observation

(1.2) (23)n​pn​(14)=∑k=0nBn−k(−k)(n≥0),\displaystyle\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n}p_{n}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}B_{n-k}^{(-k)}\qquad(n\geq 0),

where the poly-Bernoulli numbers Bm(r)B_{m}^{(r)}, r∈ℤr\in\mathbb{Z}, are defined by

∑m=0∞Bm(r)​tmm!=∑j=1∞(1−e−t)j−1jr.\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}B_{m}^{(r)}\frac{t^{m}}{m!}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{(1-e^{-t})^{j-1}}{j^{r}}.

Matsusaka [10] shows that, up to the factor 1/31/3, these anti-diagonal sums are the values of a shifted log-sine integral at non-positive integers.

1.2. Generalized Lehmer polynomials

Ikeda and Kadono [7] introduce a Hurwitz–Lerch type central binomial series and polynomials pn​(a,z)p_{n}(a,z) with pn​(1,z)=pn​(z)p_{n}(1,z)=p_{n}(z); we call them generalized Lehmer polynomials. Our variable zz corresponds to their polynomial variable xx, which is the square of the third variable in their series. The initial value is p−1​(a,z)=0p_{-1}(a,z)=0, and the defining recurrence, valid for n≥−1n\geq-1, is

(1.3) pn+1​(a,z)=2​((n+1−a)​z+a)​pn​(a,z)+2​z​(1−z)​∂zpn​(a,z)+qn​(z),\displaystyle p_{n+1}(a,z)=2((n+1-a)z+a)p_{n}(a,z)+2z(1-z)\partial_{z}p_{n}(a,z)+q_{n}(z),

with qn​(z)q_{n}(z) as above. They obtain an Eulerian polynomial expansion and a recurrence for αn​(a)≔(2/3)n​pn​(a,1/4)\alpha_{n}(a)\coloneqq(2/3)^{n}p_{n}(a,1/4). In this paper, we represent pn​(a,z)/(n+1)p_{n}(a,z)/(n+1) and αn​(a)/(n+1)\alpha_{n}(a)/(n+1) as moments; at a=1a=1, this interprets the known anti-diagonal sums probabilistically.

1.3. Moment representations

Probabilistic representations of classical polynomials include Sun’s complex moment formulas for Bernoulli and Euler polynomials and gamma moment formulas for Gegenbauer polynomials [12]. Adell and Lekuona [2] use uniform and exponential variables to represent Stirling numbers, while Adell and Bényi [1] relate potential polynomials to moments of sums of independent variables. For Eulerian polynomials, shifted negative binomial moments appear in Charalambides [6]; Barry [3] studies moment representations and Hankel transforms using exponential Riordan arrays. Liang, Mu, and Wang [9] use total positivity to obtain sufficient conditions for Catalan-like numbers to form Stieltjes moment sequences. A Stieltjes moment sequence is a real sequence (mn)n≥0(m_{n})_{n\geq 0} with mn=∫[0,∞)xn​𝑑μ​(x)m_{n}=\int_{[0,\infty)}x^{n}\,d\mu(x) for every n≥0n\geq 0, for some finite positive Borel measure μ\mu on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Our representation combines two negative binomial variables with an independent uniform variable, and it gives a necessary and sufficient condition for the normalized generalized Lehmer polynomials to form a Stieltjes moment sequence.

1.4. Main results

Set

𝒫⁡(a,z,t)≔∑n=0∞pn​(a,z)​tn+1(n+1)!,𝒬⁡(z,t)≔∑n=0∞qn−1​(z)​tnn!.\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_{n}(a,z)\frac{t^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\qquad\mathcal{Q}(z;t)\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}q_{n-1}(z)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}.

We regard 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} primarily as formal series in ℚ​[a,z]​[[t]]\mathbb{Q}[a,z][[t]], adjoining (1−z)−1(1-z)^{-1} when necessary; identities between polynomial coefficients then extend to z=1z=1. For fixed real parameters with z≠1z\neq 1, Theorem 1.2 below identifies the series with analytic germs at t=0t=0. Identities stated on larger intervals are understood through analytic continuation and do not assert Taylor convergence there.

We also fix our convention for negative binomial variables. For y>0y>0 and 0≤z<10\leq z<1, a negative binomial variable NN of shape yy and success probability 1−z1-z is a random variable with

ℙ⁡(N=m)=(y)mm!​(1−z)y​zm(m≥0),\mathbb{P}(N=m)=\frac{(y)_{m}}{m!}(1-z)^{y}z^{m}\qquad(m\geq 0),

where (b)0=1(b)_{0}=1 and (b)m=b(b+1)⋯(b+m−1)(b)_{m}=b(b+1)\cdots(b+m-1) for m≥1m\geq 1. At z=0z=0, this means that N=0N=0 almost surely. The normalization by n+1n+1 in the following theorem gives a moment sequence throughout the stated parameter range.

Theorem 1.1.

Let a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and 0≤z<10\leq z<1. Let N1,N2N_{1},N_{2} be independent negative binomial variables of shape 1/21/2 and success probability 1−z1-z, and let UU be uniform on [0,1][0,1] and independent of N1,N2N_{1},N_{2}. Define

Ya,z≔(1−z)​{2​N1+1+U⁡(2​N2+2​a−1)}.Y_{a,z}\coloneqq(1-z)\{2N_{1}+1+U(2N_{2}+2a-1)\}.

Then, for every integer n≥0n\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[Ya,zn]=pn​(a,z)n+1.\mathbb{E}[Y_{a,z}^{n}]=\frac{p_{n}(a,z)}{n+1}.

More precisely,

𝔼⁡[et​Ya,z]=𝒫⁡(a,z,t)tfor ​t∈Iz,Iz={ℝ,z=0,(−∞,log⁡(1/z)2​(1−z)),0<z<1.\mathbb{E}[e^{tY_{a,z}}]=\frac{\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)}{t}\quad\text{for }t\in I_{z},\qquad I_{z}=\begin{cases}\mathbb{R},&z=0,\\ \displaystyle\left(-\infty,\frac{\log(1/z)}{2(1-z)}\right),&0<z<1.\end{cases}

Here the quotient 𝒫⁡(a,z,t)/t\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)/t is defined at t=0t=0 by continuity and has value 11. On IzI_{z} the function 𝒫⁡(a,z,t)\mathcal{P}(a,z;t) denotes the real analytic continuation of its germ at t=0t=0, given by the integral formula in Theorem 1.2 below.

We prove Theorem 1.1 in Section 4, where we also give a mixture representation of the law of Ya,zY_{a,z} and a double-series representation of pn​(a,z)p_{n}(a,z). The following integral form of the known generating function, which we derive from the polynomial recurrences, provides a direct route to Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 1.2.

Let a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and z∈ℝ∖{1}z\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{1\}. Define

Fz​(s)≔(1−ze(z−1)​s−z)1/2.F_{z}(s)\coloneqq\left(\frac{1-z}{e^{(z-1)s}-z}\right)^{1/2}.

For tt in a neighborhood of 00, we have

𝒬⁡(z,t)=Fz​(2​t),𝒫⁡(a,z,t)=12​Fz​(2​t)​∫02​te(a−1)​(1−z)​s​Fz​(s)​𝑑s.\mathcal{Q}(z;t)=F_{z}(2t),\qquad\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)=\frac{1}{2}F_{z}(2t)\int_{0}^{2t}e^{(a-1)(1-z)s}F_{z}(s)\,ds.

The square root is the branch with value 11 at the origin.

We prove Theorem 1.2 in Section 3 and compare it there with the known hypergeometric formula. Combining Theorem 1.1 at (a,z)=(1,1/4)(a,z)=(1,1/4) with the identity (1.2) of Bényi and Matsusaka gives the following interpretation.

Corollary 1.3.

Take N1,N2,UN_{1},N_{2},U as in Theorem 1.1 with (a,z)=(1,1/4)(a,z)=(1,1/4). Set

Z1≔N1+12+U⁡(N2+12).Z_{1}\coloneqq N_{1}+\frac{1}{2}+U\left(N_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right).

Then Z1=(2/3)​Y1,1/4Z_{1}=(2/3)Y_{1,1/4}. For every integer n≥0n\geq 0,

∑k=0nBn−k(−k)=(n+1)​𝔼​[Z1n].\sum_{k=0}^{n}B_{n-k}^{(-k)}=(n+1)\mathbb{E}[Z_{1}^{n}].

In particular, the sequence ((n+1)−1​∑k=0nBn−k(−k))n≥0\bigl((n+1)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n}B_{n-k}^{(-k)}\bigr)_{n\geq 0} is a Stieltjes moment sequence.

In Section 5, we obtain negative binomial representations at a=0a=0 and a moment representation for Lehmer’s pn​(z)p_{n}(z) at a=1a=1. We also derive the recurrence for αn​(a)\alpha_{n}(a) from the differential equation in Corollary 3.2, and obtain the known Eulerian expansions from the random variable Ya,zY_{a,z}. For 0≤z<10\leq z<1, we show that the normalized sequence (pn​(a,z)/(n+1))n≥0(p_{n}(a,z)/(n+1))_{n\geq 0} is a Stieltjes moment sequence if and only if a≥0a\geq 0, and in that case we derive Hankel total non-negativity and log-convexity. Finally, we give uniform and chi-square constructions at the boundary values z=0z=0 and z=1z=1, and a moment interpretation of the polynomial contribution to Hurwitz central binomial values.

2. Preliminaries

Throughout, nn is a non-negative integer unless stated otherwise, and w≔1−zw\coloneqq 1-z. Probability statements use a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and 0≤z<10\leq z<1 unless another parameter range is specified. The first values of pn​(a,z)p_{n}(a,z), computed from the recurrence (1.3), are

p0​(a,z)\displaystyle p_{0}(a,z) =1,\displaystyle=1,
p1​(a,z)\displaystyle p_{1}(a,z) =2​(1−a)​z+2​a+1,\displaystyle=2(1-a)z+2a+1,
p2​(a,z)\displaystyle p_{2}(a,z) =4​(1−a)2​z2−2​(4​a2−3​a−5)​z+4​a2+2​a+1.\displaystyle=4(1-a)^{2}z^{2}-2(4a^{2}-3a-5)z+4a^{2}+2a+1.

The values in Table 1 agree with the table of Ikeda and Kadono [7].

For a negative binomial variable NN of shape y>0y>0 and success probability 1−z1-z with the convention fixed in Section 1, the moment generating function is

(2.1) 𝔼⁡[es​N]=(1−z1−z​es)y.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{sN}]=\left(\frac{1-z}{1-ze^{s}}\right)^{y}.

This formula holds for s<log⁡(1/z)s<\log(1/z) when 0<z<10<z<1, and for every real ss when z=0z=0.

For z≠1z\neq 1, the bivariate Eulerian polynomials are defined by

ℰ⁡(z,y,s)≔∑n=0∞En​(z,y)​snn!=(1−ze(z−1)​s−z)y.\mathcal{E}(z,y;s)\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E_{n}(z,y)\frac{s^{n}}{n!}=\left(\frac{1-z}{e^{(z-1)s}-z}\right)^{y}.

The power is the analytic branch with value 11 at s=0s=0. Each coefficient is a polynomial in z,yz,y; at z=1z=1, polynomial continuation gives En​(1,y)=(y)nE_{n}(1,y)=(y)_{n}. In particular, Fz​(s)=ℰ⁡(z,1/2,s)F_{z}(s)=\mathcal{E}(z,1/2;s). The first bivariate Eulerian polynomials are

E0​(z,y)=1,E1​(z,y)=y,E2​(z,y)=y2+z​y,E3​(z,y)=y3+3​z​y2+z2​y+z​y.E_{0}(z,y)=1,\quad E_{1}(z,y)=y,\quad E_{2}(z,y)=y^{2}+zy,\quad E_{3}(z,y)=y^{3}+3zy^{2}+z^{2}y+zy.

This family is related to the 1/k1/k-Eulerian polynomials An(k)​(z)A_{n}^{(k)}(z) of Savage and Viswanathan [11]: by their equation (6), the exponential generating function of (An(k)​(z))n≥0(A_{n}^{(k)}(z))_{n\geq 0} is ℰ⁡(z,1/k,k​s)\mathcal{E}(z,1/k;ks), so that An(k)​(z)=kn​En​(z,1/k)A_{n}^{(k)}(z)=k^{n}E_{n}(z,1/k) for positive integers kk.

To study the moment sequences arising from normalized generalized Lehmer polynomials, we recall some standard notions from the moment problem. A real sequence (mn)n≥0(m_{n})_{n\geq 0} is a Hamburger moment sequence if mn=∫ℝxn​𝑑μ​(x)m_{n}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{n}\,d\mu(x) for every n≥0n\geq 0, for some finite positive Borel measure μ\mu on ℝ\mathbb{R} with moments of all orders; it is determinate if this measure is unique. It is a Stieltjes moment sequence if such a measure can be chosen on [0,∞)[0,\infty), as in Section 1. The Hankel matrix associated with (mn)n≥0(m_{n})_{n\geq 0} is (mi+j)i,j≥0(m_{i+j})_{i,j\geq 0}. A matrix is totally non-negative if every finite minor is non-negative.

3. Generating functions

Lemma 3.1.

For the differential operator

D≔(1−2zt)∂t−2zw∂z,D\coloneqq(1-2zt)\partial_{t}-2zw\partial_{z},

we have

D​𝒬=𝒬,D​𝒫=2​a​w​𝒫+𝒬.D\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q},\qquad D\mathcal{P}=2aw\mathcal{P}+\mathcal{Q}.

Together with 𝒬⁡(z,0)=1\mathcal{Q}(z;0)=1 and 𝒫⁡(a,z,0)=0\mathcal{P}(a,z;0)=0, these equations determine the formal series uniquely.

Proof.

Multiply the recurrences (1.1) and (1.3) by tn+1/(n+1)!t^{n+1}/(n+1)! and sum over n≥−1n\geq-1. The resulting equations are

∂t𝒬\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathcal{Q} =2​z​t​∂t𝒬+𝒬+2​z​w​∂z𝒬,\displaystyle=2zt\partial_{t}\mathcal{Q}+\mathcal{Q}+2zw\partial_{z}\mathcal{Q},
∂t𝒫\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathcal{P} =2​z​t​∂t𝒫+2​a​w​𝒫+2​z​w​∂z𝒫+𝒬.\displaystyle=2zt\partial_{t}\mathcal{P}+2aw\mathcal{P}+2zw\partial_{z}\mathcal{P}+\mathcal{Q}.

Rearrangement gives the claims. Coefficient comparison recovers the original recurrences and hence proves uniqueness. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Put

Q⁡(z,t)≔Fz​(2​t)=ew​t​(w1−z​e2​w​t)1/2.Q(z,t)\coloneqq F_{z}(2t)=e^{wt}\left(\frac{w}{1-ze^{2wt}}\right)^{1/2}.

c≔2​(a−1)​w,g⁡(z,u)≔ec​u​Q​(z,u),J⁡(z,t)≔∫0tg⁡(z,u)​𝑑u.c\coloneqq 2(a-1)w,\qquad g(z,u)\coloneqq e^{cu}Q(z,u),\qquad J(z,t)\coloneqq\int_{0}^{t}g(z,u)\,du.

Since ∂zc=−2​(a−1)\partial_{z}c=-2(a-1), differentiation gives

(1−2​z​u)​∂ug−2​z​w​∂zg=(1+c)​g.(1-2zu)\partial_{u}g-2zw\partial_{z}g=(1+c)g.

Using g⁡(z,0)=1g(z,0)=1 and integrating by parts, we obtain

D​J\displaystyle DJ =(1−2zt)g(z,t)+∫0t{−(1−2zu)∂ug+(1+c)g}du\displaystyle=(1-2zt)g(z,t)+\int_{0}^{t}\{-(1-2zu)\partial_{u}g+(1+c)g\}\,du
=1+(1+c−2​z)​J=1+(2​a​w−1)​J.\displaystyle=1+(1+c-2z)J=1+(2aw-1)J.

Consequently, D⁡(Q​J)=Q+2​a​w​Q​JD(QJ)=Q+2awQJ and (Q​J)​(z,0)=0(QJ)(z,0)=0. Since 𝒬=Q\mathcal{Q}=Q, the function Q​JQJ satisfies the same equation and the same initial condition as 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Lemma 3.1, and the uniqueness in Lemma 3.1 gives

(3.1) 𝒫⁡(a,z,t)=Q⁡(z,t)​∫0te2​(a−1)​w​u​Q​(z,u)​𝑑u.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)=Q(z,t)\int_{0}^{t}e^{2(a-1)wu}Q(z,u)\,du.

The substitution s=2​us=2u proves the stated formula. The integrand is analytic near the origin, so the formal identities also hold for the corresponding analytic germs. ∎

Corollary 3.2.

For z≠1z\neq 1, the function 𝒫\mathcal{P} satisfies

(1−z​e2​w​t)​∂t𝒫=w⁡(𝒫+e2​a​w​t),𝒫⁡(a,z,0)=0.(1-ze^{2wt})\partial_{t}\mathcal{P}=w(\mathcal{P}+e^{2awt}),\qquad\mathcal{P}(a,z;0)=0.
Proof.

The identities ∂tQ/Q=w/(1−z​e2​w​t)\partial_{t}Q/Q=w/(1-ze^{2wt}) and Q2=w​e2​w​t/(1−z​e2​w​t)Q^{2}=we^{2wt}/(1-ze^{2wt}), applied to (3.1), give the result. ∎

Remark 3.3.

The equation in Corollary 3.2 is a formal identity also at z=1z=1, where it reduces to 0=00=0. At that parameter it does not determine 𝒫\mathcal{P} from its initial value.

Corollary 3.4.

For every real a,za,z, p0​(a,z)=1p_{0}(a,z)=1 and, for n≥1n\geq 1,

pn​(a,z)=pn−1​(a,z)+(2​a​w)n+z​∑j=0n−1(nj)​2n−j​wn−j−1​pj​(a,z).p_{n}(a,z)=p_{n-1}(a,z)+(2aw)^{n}+z\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}2^{n-j}w^{n-j-1}p_{j}(a,z).
Proof.

For z≠1z\neq 1, compare coefficients of tn/n!t^{n}/n! in Corollary 3.2 and divide by ww. The resulting identity is polynomial in a,za,z, so it holds also at z=1z=1. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

Let a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, 0<z<10<z<1, τ≔(1−z)​t\tau\coloneqq(1-z)t, and X≔z​e2​τX\coloneqq ze^{2\tau}. For real tt near 00,

𝒫(a,z;t)=eτ2​za−1/2​1−X∫zXua−3/2(1−u)−1/2du.\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)=\frac{e^{\tau}}{2z^{a-1/2}\sqrt{1-X}}\int_{z}^{X}u^{a-3/2}(1-u)^{-1/2}\,du.

If a>1/2a>1/2, the integral equals BX​(a−1/2,1/2)−Bz​(a−1/2,1/2)B_{X}(a-1/2,1/2)-B_{z}(a-1/2,1/2), where Bx​(α,β)=∫0xuα−1​(1−u)β−1​𝑑uB_{x}(\alpha,\beta)=\int_{0}^{x}u^{\alpha-1}(1-u)^{\beta-1}\,du.

Proof.

In Theorem 1.2, substitute s=2​v/ws=2v/w to obtain

𝒫⁡(a,z,t)=eτ1−X​∫0τe(2​a−1)​v1−z​e2​v​𝑑v.\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)=\frac{e^{\tau}}{\sqrt{1-X}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\frac{e^{(2a-1)v}}{\sqrt{1-ze^{2v}}}\,dv.

Then substituting u=z​e2​vu=ze^{2v} and simplifying the prefactor gives the result. ∎

Remark 3.6.

For a>1/2a>1/2, put

Ha​(x)≔F12​(12,a−12,a+12,x).H_{a}(x)\coloneqq{}_{2}F_{1}\left(\frac{1}{2},a-\frac{1}{2};a+\frac{1}{2};x\right).

Since Bx​(a−1/2,1/2)=xa−1/2​Ha​(x)/(a−1/2)B_{x}(a-1/2,1/2)=x^{a-1/2}H_{a}(x)/(a-1/2), Proposition 3.5 gives

𝒫⁡(a,z,t)=eτ(2​a−1)​1−X​{e(2​a−1)​τ​Ha​(X)−Ha​(z)}.\mathcal{P}(a,z;t)=\frac{e^{\tau}}{(2a-1)\sqrt{1-X}}\{e^{(2a-1)\tau}H_{a}(X)-H_{a}(z)\}.

This is the generating function obtained by Ikeda and Kadono [7] in the proof of their Eulerian polynomial representation. Thus the generating function itself is already known; our integral form and its derivation make the probabilistic factorization explicit.

The definite integral also removes apparent singularities in the parameter. For 0<z,X<10<z,X<1, its expansion, with α=a−1/2\alpha=a-1/2, is

∫zXuα−1(1−u)−1/2du=∑k=0∞(1/2)kk!Xα+k−zα+kα+k.\int_{z}^{X}u^{\alpha-1}(1-u)^{-1/2}\,du=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(1/2)_{k}}{k!}\frac{X^{\alpha+k}-z^{\alpha+k}}{\alpha+k}.

At α=−k\alpha=-k, the quotient is log⁡(X/z)\log(X/z). The binomial series for (1−u)−1/2(1-u)^{-1/2} converges uniformly on the interval between zz and XX, which justifies termwise integration for every complex α\alpha. Each term of the resulting series is entire in α\alpha, and the series converges locally uniformly in α\alpha. Hence the integral is entire in α\alpha, and any poles of the separate incomplete beta terms cancel.

Remark 4.2.

Since 𝒫⁡(a,z,0)=0\mathcal{P}(a,z;0)=0, 𝒫\mathcal{P} itself is not a moment generating function. Its derivative satisfies

The derivative need not be a moment generating function: at (a,z)=(1,0)(a,z)=(1,0), its proposed first two moments are 33 and 77, giving the negative variance 7−32=−27-3^{2}=-2. Indeed, N1=N2=0N_{1}=N_{2}=0 almost surely at z=0z=0, so Y1,0=1+UY_{1,0}=1+U, and Theorem 1.1 gives p1​(1,0)=2​𝔼​[1+U]=3p_{1}(1,0)=2\mathbb{E}[1+U]=3 and p2​(1,0)=3​𝔼​[(1+U)2]=7p_{2}(1,0)=3\mathbb{E}[(1+U)^{2}]=7. At a=0a=0, however, it is a moment generating function, as shown below.

Remark 5.2.

The identity for general yy is already contained in the series expansion of Savage and Viswanathan [11], equation (9). It also follows from Charalambides [6], equation (3.4), by setting α=0,β=y\alpha=0,\beta=y in his polynomial An​(z,α,β)A_{n}(z;\alpha,\beta); his positive-parameter formula extends continuously to α=0\alpha=0. The negative binomial interpretation is therefore already known. The identity pn​(0,z)=qn​(z)p_{n}(0,z)=q_{n}(z) is also noted by Ikeda and Kadono [7]; it does not extend to n=−1n=-1.

Corollary 5.6.

Fix a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and 0≤z<10\leq z<1, and set mn=pn​(a,z)/(n+1)m_{n}=p_{n}(a,z)/(n+1). The sequence (mn)n≥0(m_{n})_{n\geq 0} is a determinate Hamburger moment sequence (see Section 2). It is a Stieltjes moment sequence if and only if a≥0a\geq 0. In that case the Hankel matrix (mi+j)i,j≥0(m_{i+j})_{i,j\geq 0} has all minors non-negative and

mn2≤mn−1​mn+1(n≥1).m_{n}^{2}\leq m_{n-1}m_{n+1}\qquad(n\geq 1).

The law μ\mu of Ya,zY_{a,z} represents the moments and, by the estimate in the proof of Theorem 1.1, satisfies ∫ℝeε​|x|​𝑑μ​(x)<∞\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\varepsilon|x|}\,d\mu(x)<\infty for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. ∫cosh⁡(ε​x)​𝑑ν​(x)=∑n=0∞ε2​n​m2​n(2​n)!=∫cosh⁡(ε​x)​𝑑μ​(x)<∞.\int\cosh(\varepsilon x)\,d\nu(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\varepsilon^{2n}m_{2n}}{(2n)!}=\int\cosh(\varepsilon x)\,d\mu(x)<\infty.

Since eε​|x|≤2​cosh⁡(ε​x)e^{\varepsilon|x|}\leq 2\cosh(\varepsilon x), both measures have finite absolute exponential moments. Their moment generating functions are analytic on |Re⁡(t)|<ε|\ReNew(t)|<\varepsilon and have the same Taylor coefficients at 00. By the identity theorem, these functions coincide throughout the strip and hence on the imaginary axis. Their characteristic functions therefore coincide, and uniqueness of characteristic functions implies μ=ν\mu=\nu.

The mixture in Corollary 4.1 is supported on [0,∞)[0,\infty) when a≥0a\geq 0. If a<0a<0, the event N1=N2=0N_{1}=N_{2}=0 has probability ww, and on it Ya,z=w⁡{1+(2​a−1)​U}Y_{a,z}=w\{1+(2a-1)U\}. Hence

The log-convexity inequality follows from Cauchy–Schwarz applied to Ya,z(n−1)/2Y_{a,z}^{(n-1)/2} and Ya,z(n+1)/2Y_{a,z}^{(n+1)/2}. ∎
